blanks.sentence: Email is common in modern workplaces, and most people try to make their messages sound _____.
One listener dislikes emails that begin with only a name and no simple _____.
This unnecessary formality can make the reader feel immediately _____.
Another example of rude email behaviour was replying to a careful message with a single _____.
Such rude email behaviour is described as _____.
A fight response may involve dominance or _____ of other people.
One hostile email tactic is copying in _____ to escalate the issue.
By contrast, a flight response involves self-protection through _____ or avoidance.
To get something “off your plate” means moving a task away from your own _____.
People are more likely to be uncivil when they are _____.

multipleChoice.question: What workplace issue is introduced at the start?
options: Some emails can feel impolite despite efforts to be polite
Most workers no longer use email professionally
Rude emails are mainly a problem outside work
Email has become less important in modern offices

multipleChoice.question: Why does the opening style of some emails annoy one listener?
options: It contains too many friendly phrases
It includes a long personal introduction
It asks for a reply too quickly
It feels unnecessarily formal and threatening

multipleChoice.question: What does the single-emoji example show?
options: Emojis are always unacceptable at work
A minimal reply can feel disrespectful after a careful message
Carefully written emails are usually unclear
Anonymous messages are more polite than signed ones

multipleChoice.question: What does “put someone on the defensive” mean here?
options: Make someone eager to continue the exchange
Force someone to answer every point in detail
Make someone feel threatened or unsure
Encourage someone to use a warmer greeting

multipleChoice.question: How are the two early email examples classified?
options: As uncivil forms of communication
As formal but acceptable workplace habits
As examples of efficient messaging
As unavoidable technical problems

multipleChoice.question: How does Emma Russell distinguish fight and flight responses in emails?
options: Fight means ignoring emails; flight means copying senior people
Fight means apologising; flight means writing more politely
Fight attacks or dominates; flight withdraws or avoids
Fight happens only to managers; flight happens only to junior staff

multipleChoice.question: In the example of a fight response, what does the boss do?
options: Refuses to answer all points in an email
Deletes the worker’s message without reading it
Asks the worker to delay a deadline
Gives someone else credit for the worker’s work

multipleChoice.question: What does “get work off their plate” refer to?
options: Finishing every task carefully before replying
Passing tasks or problems to someone else
Refusing to receive emails from colleagues
Organising work into a clearer schedule

multipleChoice.question: Why are people more likely to behave uncivilly in email?
options: They are working in stressful, frazzled environments
They prefer short messages to long ones
They have stopped using workplace greetings altogether
They believe rude emails save money

multipleChoice.question: What practical advice is given for writing an angry email?
options: Copy in senior staff before sending
Reply with an emoji to reduce tension
Pause before pressing send
Avoid answering any of the email’s points
